notes.title: PyObject, Refcounts & the Object Header
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Data model: objects, values and types · 📘 C API: common object structures · 📘 sys.getsizeof · 📜 PEP 683: Immortal objects · 🔬 Ten Thousand Meters: the object system · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Memory management in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Every Python value is a box: 16 bytes of header (refcount + type pointer), then the payload. Names and containers hold pointers to boxes, never the values themselves.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What's in every PyObject header? ob_refcnt (8 B) and ob_type (8 B); variable-size objects add ob_size.
Why is a float 24 bytes? 16-byte header + 8-byte double.
What does a list slot hold? An 8-byte pointer to a separate object.
Is sys.getsizeof deep? No: shallow; includes the GC header, not referenced objects.
What changed in 3.12? PEP 683 immortal objects: None, small ints … have a fixed refcount.
1M floats: list vs array('d')? ~32.4 MB vs ~8.2 MB (tracemalloc, CPython 3.12.13).

💡 The idea

Why does a list of a million floats use about 32 MB when a million doubles should be 8? Ask Python how big things really are:

import sys
sys.getsizeof(1234.5)                 # → 24     an 8-byte double in a 24-byte object
sys.getsizeof([1.5, 2.5])             # → 72
sys.getsizeof(["x" * 1_000_000])      # → 64     a 1 MB string inside...
sys.getsizeof([0])                    # → 64     ...costs the same as a 0

A list holding a megabyte string is the same size as a list holding 0, so the list can't contain its elements: it holds 8-byte pointers to separate objects, each with its own header. On CPython 3.12.13 a list of a million floats measures ~32.4 MB under tracemalloc; an array('d') of raw doubles is ~8.2 MB.

The trade: values can go anywhere and containers hold anything, and you pay by boxing every value in its own heap object with a header, reached through a pointer.

⚙️ How it works

Every CPython object starts with the same prefix, which is what lets the interpreter handle any value as a PyObject *:

ob_refcnt drives lifetime. Every new reference (a name, a list slot, an argument) increments it; every dropped one decrements it. In CPython, reaching zero calls the type's deallocator on the spot, so memory is usually freed the instant the last reference goes (#28).

ob_type drives behaviour. x + y follows x's type pointer to the type object and calls its add slot, so even 1 + 1 is a pointer chase, a slot call and usually a new box for the result. Variable-length types (int, tuple) add ob_size; an int stores 30-bit digits, so it grows: 28 bytes up to 2**30 - 1, then 32, then 36 by 2**63.

Containers carry a hidden GC header. Objects that can reference others (lists, dicts, instances) can form cycles, so the cyclic collector tracks them (#29) via a 16-byte header in front of the object: [].__sizeof__() is 40, sys.getsizeof([]) is 56. A float isn't tracked.

Some objects are shared or immortal. CPython pre-allocates ints −5 to 256. Since 3.12 (PEP 683), None, True, False, small ints and others are immortal: their refcount is pinned and never written, which matters for copy-on-write after fork and for free-threaded builds.

💻 Code

Measure the real, deep cost of a data shape with tracemalloc, never getsizeof:

import tracemalloc
from array import array

def traced_mb(build):
    """Bytes the allocator hands out while build() runs: deep, not shallow."""
    tracemalloc.start()
    before = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0]
    obj = build()                                    # keep it alive while measuring
    after = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0]
    tracemalloc.stop()
    return round((after - before) / 1e6, 1), obj

N = 1_000_000
print(traced_mb(lambda: [float(i) for i in range(N)])[0])               # → 32.4  N boxes + N pointers
print(traced_mb(lambda: array("d", (float(i) for i in range(N))))[0])   # → 8.2   raw doubles

sys.getsizeof on the list would report ~8 MB and hide the 24 MB of float objects, which is how capacity estimates come out four times too small.

⚠️ Break it: watch the refcount field move.

import sys
x = 1234.5                    # a float outside any cache
print(sys.getrefcount(x))     # baseline (+1 for getrefcount's own argument)
y = x
print(sys.getrefcount(x))
del y
print(sys.getrefcount(x), sys.getrefcount(None))
# look for: +1 on y = x, −1 on del y; None reports a huge fixed number
# naive model predicts: y = x copies the value, so x's count never moves

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints 4, 5, then 4 4294967295 (the baseline depends on references the interpreter itself holds; the +1/−1 is what matters). Assignment copies a pointer into the same header, and None's count is a sentinel refcounting never touches.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Every CPython object starts with a reference count and a type pointer; variable-length types add a size. The refcount drives memory management: at zero the object is freed immediately. The type pointer drives behaviour: every operation dispatches through it. That uniform header lets the interpreter treat any value as a PyObject *, and the cost is overhead: a float is 24 bytes for 8 bytes of data, each one a separate heap box.

Q · Mechanism — What happens to memory and refcounts on b = a, then del a, then del b? b = a copies the pointer and increments ob_refcnt; nothing else is copied. del a removes the name and decrements; the object survives because b refers to it. del b decrements again, and at zero CPython calls tp_dealloc on that line: the object's own references are released, possibly cascading, and memory returns to the allocator. On 3.12, immortal objects never reach zero, so binding and deleting None changes nothing.

Q · Failure — A pure-Python numeric loop is slow and NumPy makes it dramatically faster. What does boxing cost, and what did NumPy change? In Python, total += x * y dispatches * through the type pointer, allocates a new 24-byte float, adjusts refcounts, then repeats for +=; elements are scattered heap boxes, so the cache helps less. The arithmetic is a sliver of the work. NumPy stores raw doubles contiguously under one header and runs one compiled loop per call, with no per-element dispatch, allocation or refcounts. Same story for memory: ~32 MB as a list, 8 MB as float64.

Q · Design — Tens of millions of small records (id, score, timestamp) must fit in RAM under a tight container limit. How do you reason about it? Price the shape first, because overhead multiplies. On CPython 3.12, 100,000 two-field instances measured ~12.0 MB, with __slots__ ~8.8 MB, as tuples ~9.6 MB: mostly headers and boxes for ~20 bytes of data each. __slots__ is the first step, not the answer. The real move is columnar: one array('q') or NumPy array per field, so each record costs its raw bytes; shared across workers, a memory-mapped Arrow file. Watch RSS per worker against the limit, broken down by tracemalloc allocation site.

⚖️ Compare

Storage for 1M floats What's stored tracemalloc (3.12.13) Reading an element
list 1M pointers + 1M 24 B floats ~32.4 MB returns the existing object
tuple same, no over-allocation ≈ list returns the existing object
array('d') 1M raw doubles, one header ~8.2 MB boxes a new float per read
NumPy float64 1M raw doubles, one header ~8 MB vectorised ops never box

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "sys.getsizeof(obj) is how much memory obj uses"
    ✅ It's shallow: one box, not what it points to.
    ↳ Proof: sys.getsizeof(["x" * 10**6]) is 64 bytes.
    ↳ Fix: tracemalloc for the real, deep cost.
  • 🪞 "A list of numbers is an array of numbers"
    ✅ It's an array of pointers to separately allocated number objects.
    ↳ Why it matters: each has its own 16-byte header, so floats cost ~4× an array('d').
  • ❌ "sys.getrefcount(x) counts the variables pointing at x"
    ✅ It counts every reference: list slots, dict values, frames, its own argument (+1).
    ↳ Also: on 3.12 it returns a fixed sentinel for immortal objects like None.
  • 🔀 Not the same as __dict__ / __slots__
    ↳ Difference: the header is the fixed prefix every object has, even an int; __dict__ vs __slots__ is where an instance keeps attributes, after the header.
    ↳ So: __slots__ can remove the dict; nothing removes the header.
  • ⚠️ Don't optimise object overhead for data you hold in thousands.
    ↳ Why: at that scale the header is noise; it only dominates at millions of objects.
    ↳ Instead: readable code until a profile says otherwise.
  • ⚠️ Don't use array as a speed trick for element-by-element loops.
    ↳ Why: every read boxes a new float, so it's smaller but not faster.
    ↳ Instead: vectorised NumPy operations for speed.
  • 🔖 Version: 3.12 added immortal objects and a new int layout (sys.getsizeof(0) is 28 on 3.12, 24 on 3.10).
    ↳ Also: free-threaded 3.13+ (PEP 703) splits the refcount; all numbers here are CPython 3.12.13 on macOS arm64, so re-measure.

🔗 Links

notes.title: dict Internals
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Mapping types: dict · 📘 Data model: __hash__ · 📜 PEP 412: Key-sharing dictionary · 📜 PEP 456: SipHash · 🔬 Ten Thousand Meters: how dictionaries work · 📖 Inside Python dict: an explorable explanation

⚡ TL;DR

A dict is a sparse index into a dense, insertion-ordered list of (hash, key, value). Its O(1) is borrowed from the key's hash: a bad hash makes it linear, and deletes never shrink it.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
How does d[key] find a slot? hash(key) & mask into the index array; collisions use perturbed probing.
Why are dicts ordered? Compact layout (3.6): dense entries in insertion order; guaranteed since 3.7.
When does a dict resize? At 2/3 full; rebuilds everything at a larger power of two.
Does deleting keys free memory? No: tombstones, no shrink; rebuild with dict(d).
Collision check order? Identity (is) → stored hash equal → __eq__.
Chaining or open addressing? Open addressing; linked buckets are the Java answer.

💡 The idea

Why must a dict key be hashable, and why can two different keys collide? Because a dict never compares your key against every key it holds. It computes a number from the key and jumps:

{[1, 2]: "x"}            # → TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
d = {1: "int"}
d[1.0] = "float"
d[True] = "bool"
d                        # → {1: 'bool'}

A list can't be a key because if it changed after insertion its hash would change and the dict would look in the wrong place. And hash(1) == hash(1.0) == hash(True) with 1 == 1.0 == True, so all three writes hit one slot: the first key object is kept, only the value changes.

indices (sparse, 8/16/32… slots)    [ -, 0, -, -, 2, -, 1, - ]
entries (dense, insertion order)    0:(h,"apple",1.2)  1:(h,"pear",0.8)  2:(h,"kiwi",2.5)

The trade: O(1) average lookup, paid for with a mostly empty index table and a demand that every key have a stable, well-spread hash; it quietly gets slow when that demand isn't met.

⚙️ How it works

A lookup is hash, mask, probe, then a cheap-first comparison:

Open addressing with perturbed probing. The table size is a power of two, so the low bits of the hash pick a start slot. On a collision, CPython probes another slot in the same table with a recurrence that mixes in higher hash bits, so keys sharing low bits spread out fast. At each occupied slot it checks is, then the stored hash, and only then calls __eq__, which is why __eq__ and __hash__ must agree (#4a).

Compact layout: sparse index, dense entries. In CPython 3.6+, index slots are 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes depending on table size; each entry is three 8-byte words with no gaps. The emptiness lives in the cheap array, so dicts got smaller, and iteration walks the dense array, so order came for free.

Resize at two-thirds; deletes leave tombstones. On CPython 3.12 an empty dict is 64 bytes, the first insert makes it 224, and it grows at the 6th, 11th and 22nd keys; each O(n) rebuild gets rarer, so inserts stay amortised O(1). Deleting can't empty an index slot without breaking other keys' probe chains, so it leaves a dummy, and the dict never shrinks until a rebuild.

Hashes are cached and randomised; instances share keys. str caches its hash, and str/bytes use per-process salted SipHash (siphash13 on 3.12) against hash-flooding. Instances of one class share a keys table (PEP 412), and since 3.11 most keep values inline with no dict until you touch __dict__.

💻 Code

A composite cache key, and eviction that actually frees memory:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)     # frozen → __hash__ from all fields, matching __eq__
class CacheKey:
    tenant: str
    model: str
    prompt_sha: str                     # hash the prompt once; don't key on 50 KB of text

cache: dict[CacheKey, str] = {}

def get_completion(tenant, model, prompt_sha):
    return cache.get(CacheKey(tenant, model, prompt_sha))   # one hash, usually one probe

def evict_tenant(tenant):
    global cache
    cache = {k: v for k, v in cache.items() if k.tenant != tenant}   # rebuild: sized for what's left

Deleting in a loop would leave the table at its peak size; the rebuilt dict is sized for the survivors.

⚠️ Break it: a legal but terrible hash.

import time
class Key:
    eq_calls = 0
    def __init__(self, v): self.v = v
    def __hash__(self): return 42                # equal objects hash equal... but all collide
    def __eq__(self, other): Key.eq_calls += 1; return self.v == other.v
t = time.perf_counter()
d = {Key(i): i for i in range(1000)}
print(Key.eq_calls, f"{(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.1f} ms")
# look for: ~500,000 __eq__ calls to insert 1,000 keys
# naive model predicts: ~0 __eq__ calls, O(1) per insert

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints 500300 and about 40 ms, against ~0.03 ms with int keys. O(1) is a property of well-spread hashes, not of dicts: here every insert probes past every key already present, so the build is quadratic.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Python hashes the key, masks it to a slot in a power-of-two table, and looks there. Empty means absent. Occupied means it checks identity, then the stored hash, then __eq__; on a mismatch it probes another slot with a perturbed sequence. With a well-spread hash that's one or two probes, so lookup is O(1) on average, and it's why keys must be hashable and hash consistently with equality.

Q · Mechanism — Explain the compact layout. Why did it make dicts both smaller and ordered? Before 3.6 a dict was one sparse array of (hash, key, value) entries, three words each, and about a third was always empty, so the empty slots cost 24 bytes apiece. 3.6 split it into a sparse indices array of tiny integers and a dense entries array. The emptiness moved to the cheap array, so memory dropped. New entries append to the dense array and iteration walks it, so order is insertion order; 3.7 made that a guarantee. Re-inserting a deleted key moves it to the end.

Q · Failure — A dict-heavy service is slow, and the profiler shows most time in __eq__ on a custom key class. What's happening? __eq__ is hot because many occupied slots have a matching stored hash but the wrong key: the hash isn't spreading keys. Typical causes are hashing a low-cardinality field (only tenant), a constant hash, or a field most keys share; k keys on one hash make each operation O(k) and the build O(k²) (see Break it). Fix: hash exactly the fields __eq__ compares, hash((self.a, self.b)), or let @dataclass(frozen=True) generate it. A mutable key whose hashed fields change is worse: silent data loss.

Q · Design — A per-process cache of a few million entries sits on the request path. Where do dict internals bite, and how do you design around them? Memory binds. Growth is step-shaped: after a resize the index is a third full, and each resize briefly holds old and new tables, a latency and memory spike on the triggering request. Deletes never shrink, so eviction by del keeps peak size forever. Size capacity from the post-resize high-water mark, evict by rebuilding survivors or use a bounded LRU/TTL cache, keep keys small and cheap to hash, and measure keys and values with tracemalloc. Watch RSS stepping up with no matching growth in entry count.

⚖️ Compare

dict set list of pairs OrderedDict
Lookup by key O(1) average O(1) membership O(n) O(1) average
Ordered insertion (3.7+) no yes yes + move_to_end
Shrinks after deletes no, until rebuild no yes no
Worst case O(n) per op with collisions same O(n) same
Use for mapping, caches, indexes membership, dedup tiny data LRU via move_to_end

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Dict operations are always O(1)"
    ✅ O(1) on average with a well-spread hash.
    ↳ Why: colliding hashes make each operation O(n) and the build O(n²) (see Break it).
  • 🪞 "Deleting entries from a big dict gives the memory back"
    ✅ Deletes leave tombstones; the table keeps its size.
    ↳ Proof: deleting 9 of 10 keys leaves sys.getsizeof unchanged.
    ↳ Fix: rebuild with dict(d) or a comprehension.
  • ❌ "1, 1.0 and True are three different keys"
    ✅ They hash equal and compare equal: one key.
    ↳ Symptom: the first key object is kept; later writes only replace the value.
  • 🔀 Not the same as "sorted" or OrderedDict
    ↳ Difference: a dict keeps insertion order, not key order; OrderedDict adds order manipulation and order-sensitive equality.
    ↳ Example: {"a": 1, "b": 2} == {"b": 2, "a": 1} is True for plain dicts.
  • ⚠️ Don't use keys whose hashed fields can change.
    ↳ Why: the dict looks in the wrong slot, so the entry is unreachable but still holds memory and still iterates.
    ↳ Instead: frozen dataclasses or tuples.
  • ⚠️ Don't hand-roll __hash__ over a subset of the __eq__ fields, or low-cardinality fields.
    ↳ Why: it's legal, so nothing complains, and lookups quietly turn linear.
    ↳ Instead: hash((self.a, self.b)) over exactly the compared fields.
  • 🔖 Version: compact dicts 3.6, order guaranteed 3.7, key sharing 3.3, inline instance values 3.11+.
    ↳ Also: siphash13 on 3.12 (was siphash24 before 3.11); sizes here are CPython 3.12.13, re-measure.

🔗 Links

notes.title: set / frozenset Internals
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Set types: set, frozenset

⚡ TL;DR

A set is a dict with no values: hashed membership, no duplicates, no order. frozenset is the one you can hash.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
x in set vs x in list? O(1) average (hash + probe) vs O(n) scan.
Is a set ordered? No: iteration follows table position, not insertion (unlike dict).
set vs frozenset? frozenset is immutable and hashable: a dict key or set element.

💡 The idea

Membership on a list scans, so x in items inside a loop is quietly O(n²). A set is the dict hash table without values: x in s hashes and probes, O(1) on average. CPython's set doesn't use dict's compact layout, so iteration has no insertion order and, for strings, varies with the hash seed. The cost is memory: 216 bytes empty on CPython 3.12, growing in big steps.

💻 Code

allowed = {"read", "write"}
print("admin" in allowed)                     # → False   hash + probe, no scan
seen = set(); dupes = [x for x in [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] if x in seen or seen.add(x)]
print(dupes)                                  # → [3, 1]   second occurrences
perms = {frozenset({"read"}): "viewer"}       # frozenset is hashable → a key
print(perms[frozenset({"read"})])             # → viewer

notes.title: list Internals
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Sequence types: list · 📘 collections.deque · 📘 Python Wiki: TimeComplexity · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Python lists

⚡ TL;DR

A list is a contiguous array of pointers with room to spare at the right end. The right end and indexing are O(1); anything at the front is O(n), which is what deque is for.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a list physically store? A contiguous C array of PyObject *, plus length and capacity.
Why is append amortised O(1)? Proportional over-allocation (~12.5% + a constant) makes resizes rare.
Cost of pop(0) / insert(0, x)? O(n): every later pointer shifts; use deque.popleft() / appendleft().
Why does [[0]*3]*3 alias? * repeats one inner list's pointer three times.
Does a list shrink after pops? Yes, below half capacity (unlike a dict).
Capacity sequence from empty (3.12)? 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76.

💡 The idea

A million appends take a fraction of a second, and events[500_000] is instant. So insert, pop(0) and in must be cheap too, right? Watch the size and the front:

import sys, timeit
lst, sizes = [], set()
for i in range(20):
    lst.append(i); sizes.add(sys.getsizeof(lst))
sorted(sizes)                                       # → [88, 120, 184, 248]
timeit.timeit("l.pop(0); l.append(0)", setup="l = list(range(10_000))", number=10_000)    # → ~0.007 s
timeit.timeit("l.pop(0); l.append(0)", setup="l = list(range(100_000))", number=10_000)   # → ~0.12 s

The size jumps and then stays flat: each jump is a bigger pointer array, the flat stretches fill spare slots. And ten times the data made pop(0) more than ten times slower per call, because every remaining pointer shifts down one slot.

The trade: O(1) indexing and amortised O(1) append, by storing pointers contiguously with spare room at the end, paid for with O(n) for anything that happens anywhere else.

⚙️ How it works

A CPython list is a header, a length, a capacity and a pointer to a separate C array of PyObject *. The append path:

Indexing is pointer arithmetic. lst[i] is ob_item[i], one memory read whatever the length, possible because slots are contiguous and all 8 bytes.

Growth is proportional, not doubling. When full, CPython reallocates to (n + (n >> 3) + 6) & ~3: about 12.5% headroom plus a constant, a multiple of 4. Because headroom grows with the list, resizes over n appends are logarithmic and total copying is O(n), so appends are amortised O(1). Lists also shrink when the length drops below half the capacity.

The front costs a memmove. insert(0, x), pop(0) and del lst[0] shift every later pointer, so they're O(n). remove, in and index are O(n) scans comparing with ==. A list built at a known size (list(range(10)), 136 bytes on 3.12) is exact; one grown by appends keeps headroom ([i for i in range(10)], 184 bytes).

Slots hold pointers; sort is Timsort. Repeating a list repeats pointers, which is the [[0] * 3] * 3 trap. list.sort() is stable Timsort, close to O(n) on nearly sorted data, with a powersort merge policy since 3.11.

💻 Code

Pick the structure by which end you touch and what you store:

from collections import deque
from array import array

pending: deque[str] = deque()            # FIFO queue: never list.pop(0)
pending.append("job-1")                  # O(1) at the right
job = pending.popleft()                  # O(1) at the left

window: deque[float] = deque(maxlen=1_000)   # last N latencies, oldest evicted for you
for ms in (12.0, 15.5, 9.8):
    window.append(ms)
p50 = sorted(window)[len(window) // 2]   # sort a copy only when you need the stat

samples = array("d", (0.0 for _ in range(1_000_000)))   # unboxed: ~8 MB, not ~32 MB

A list is the default for "grow at the end, index anywhere, iterate"; front pops mean deque, large numeric data means array or NumPy.

⚠️ Break it: build a grid with *.

grid = [[0] * 3] * 3
grid[0][0] = 1
print(grid)
print(grid[0] is grid[1] is grid[2])
safe = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
safe[0][0] = 1
print(safe)
# look for: 1 in EVERY row of grid, and the is-check True
# naive model predicts: [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints [[1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0]], True, then [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]. * 3 repeated the pointer to one row; the comprehension builds three.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A CPython list is a dynamic array of pointers: length, capacity, and a contiguous C array of PyObject *, each pointing at an element elsewhere on the heap. Indexing is one read, so O(1). Appends are amortised O(1) through proportional over-allocation. Anything at the front, plus in and remove, is O(n). Slots are pointers, which is why lists hold mixed types and why [[0]*3]*3 gives three references to one row.

Q · Mechanism — Why is append amortised O(1), and what's CPython's growth policy? When the array is full, CPython reallocates to roughly n + n/8 + 6, rounded to a multiple of 4: on 3.12, capacities 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76. Most appends write into a spare slot; the occasional one pays a realloc that may copy every pointer. Because headroom is proportional, resizes are logarithmic in n and total copying is linear, so each append averages O(1); individual resizes are still O(n) spikes. The ~12.5% is smaller than textbook doubling: more resizes, less stranded memory.

Q · Failure — A FIFO work queue uses append and pop(0), and throughput collapses as the backlog grows. Why, and what's the fix? pop(0) memmoves the whole array, so each dequeue is O(backlog). Small backlogs hide it; under load the consumer slows, the backlog grows, and each pop gets slower: a feedback loop that looks like a cliff. On CPython 3.12, pop(0) costs ~0.7 µs at 10k and ~12 µs at 100k, while deque.popleft() stays ~0.014 µs. Fix: deque; across threads queue.Queue, across tasks asyncio.Queue.

Q · Design — An in-process buffer keeps the last N minutes of events for rolling metrics and flushes batches downstream. List, deque or array, and where does each break? It appends right and evicts left, so not a list. A deque fits: maxlen for count windows, or pop-left-while-older-than-cutoff for time windows, amortised O(1). Memory breaks next: thirty million boxed events at 50k/s for ten minutes. Pre-aggregate: array('d') ring buffers or HDR/t-digest sketches make memory O(buckets). Past that, per-process buffers give per-worker percentiles, so raw events belong in Kafka or Redis Streams. Watch per-worker RSS against event rate.

⚖️ Compare

list tuple deque array('d') / NumPy
Index x[i] O(1) O(1) O(1) at ends, O(n) mid O(1)
Append right amortised O(1) immutable O(1) amortised O(1) / NumPy copies
Pop / insert left O(n) — O(1) O(n)
Stores pointers + headroom pointers, exact pointers in 64-slot blocks raw values, one type
Best for general sequences fixed records, keys queues, windows large numeric data

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A list operation is a list operation; they're all fast"
    ✅ Only indexing and the right end are O(1).
    ↳ Why: insert(0), pop(0), remove, in and index are O(n), and the syntax gives no hint which is which.
  • 🪞 "CPython lists double when they fill up"
    ✅ They grow about 12.5% plus a constant (4 → 8 → 16 → 24 → 32 → 40 → 52 on 3.12).
    ↳ So: still amortised O(1), with less wasted headroom than doubling.
  • ❌ "[[0] * 3] * 3 makes a 3×3 grid"
    ✅ It makes one row and three pointers to it (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)].
  • 🔀 Not the same as a linked list
    ↳ Difference: a Python list is a dynamic array (O(1) index, O(n) front); deque is the linked structure (blocks), which is why their trade-offs mirror each other.
  • ⚠️ Don't use a list as a queue.
    ↳ Why: pop(0) is O(n), and backlogs grow exactly when load is high.
    ↳ Instead: deque, or queue.Queue / asyncio.Queue across threads or tasks.
  • ⚠️ Don't test membership in a big list inside a loop.
    ↳ Why: each x in lst is a linear scan: ~258 µs for a 100k miss vs ~0.006 µs in a set (3.12).
    ↳ Instead: build a set once.
  • 🔖 Version: the growth formula and byte counts here are CPython 3.12.13, arm64; Timsort uses powersort since 3.11.
    ↳ Free-threaded 3.13+: single list ops take a per-object lock, but check-then-act still needs your own lock.

notes.title: str Internals
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Text sequence type: str · 📜 PEP 393: Flexible string representation · 📘 sys.intern · 📖 Ten Thousand Meters: how Python strings work

⚡ TL;DR

A string is immutable and stored at one fixed width, 1, 2 or 4 bytes, set by its widest character. So indexing is O(1) and the hash is cached, but every change is a copy: build with join, not +=.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
PEP 393 in one line? All chars at 1, 2 or 4 bytes: the narrowest width the widest char allows.
Why is s += t in a loop risky? Each concat copies → O(n²); the in-place shortcut needs a sole reference.
Linear way to build a string? Collect pieces in a list, then "".join(parts).
Are strings interned automatically? Identifier-like constants and names are; runtime strings aren't, unless sys.intern().
str vs bytes? Code points vs raw octets; encode/decode only at I/O boundaries.
len("😀") vs its UTF-8 size? 1 code point, 4 bytes.

💡 The idea

Why do three strings of the same length have three different sizes?

import sys
sys.getsizeof("a" * 100), sys.getsizeof("€" * 100), sys.getsizeof("😀" * 100)   # → (141, 258, 460)
sys.getsizeof("a" * 1000), sys.getsizeof("a" * 1000 + "😀")                    # → (1041, 4064)

ASCII costs 1 byte per character, € 2, an emoji 4, and the width applies to the whole string: one emoji turned a thousand 1-byte characters into a thousand and one 4-byte ones. And because strings are immutable, s += "!" can't append: it builds a new string with both halves and rebinds s.

The trade: immutability plus one fixed width per string gives O(1) indexing, safe sharing and a cached hash, and makes every modification a copy, with the whole string paying for its widest character.

⚙️ How it works

At creation, CPython scans for the highest code point and picks the narrowest width that fits every character:

One width per string (PEP 393, 3.3+). Fixed width makes s[i] pointer arithmetic and len(s) a stored field, both O(1). On CPython 3.12 a pure-ASCII string has a 40-byte header plus one byte per character plus a NUL, so sys.getsizeof("") is 41 (49 before 3.12, when PEP 623 removed a legacy field).

Immutability makes the rest cheap. The hash is computed once and cached, so a string key hashes once for its lifetime; strings share across threads without locks; identical strings can be interned. The compiler interns identifier-like constants and names, so lookups hit the identity fast path (#21); runtime-built strings aren't interned unless you call sys.intern().

Concatenation copies, with a fragile shortcut. a + b allocates the combined length at the wider kind and copies both, so n appends copy ~n²/2 characters. In CPython, s += t resizes in place when s's refcount shows the local is its only reference, making the loop roughly linear. Any other reference, an attribute target, or PyPy silently disables it. "".join(parts) sizes once and copies once everywhere.

str is text, bytes is data. A str holds code points with no encoding; bytes holds octets. "a" + b"b" raises TypeError, so conversion is explicit, with encode/decode at I/O edges.

💻 Code

Linear building, one encode at the edge, and normalised keys:

import unicodedata

def render_report(rows) -> bytes:
    parts: list[str] = []                       # collect pieces; never s += in a loop
    for r in rows:
        parts.append(f"{r['id']}\t{r['name']}\t{r['score']:.2f}\n")
    return "".join(parts).encode("utf-8")       # one copy, then str → bytes once, at the boundary

def canonical_key(user_text: str) -> str:
    # "é" can be one code point or "e" + a combining accent: normalise before keying
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", user_text).casefold()

assert "é" != "é"                                  # look identical, aren't equal
assert canonical_key("Café") == canonical_key("CAFÉ")

casefold() is the Unicode-correct version of lower() for caseless comparison.

⚠️ Break it: defeat the in-place += shortcut with one extra reference.

import time
def build(n, keep_alias):
    s = ""
    for _ in range(n):
        if keep_alias: prev = s       # one extra reference to the current string
        s += "x"
for n in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):
    t = time.perf_counter(); build(n, False); a = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); build(n, True);  b = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(n, f"{a * 1000:.1f} ms", f"{b * 1000:.1f} ms")
# look for: right column ~quadruples as n doubles; left ~doubles
# naive model predicts: an unused `prev = s` can't change the cost

On CPython 3.12.13 it printed about 1.4 / 14 ms, 2.7 / 87 ms, 5.4 / 333 ms. The alias made the refcount 2, so every += became a full copy: the textbook O(n²).

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Strings are immutable: every "change" creates a new string and rebinds the name. That lets CPython cache the hash, share strings without locks, and intern identical ones. Since PEP 393 each string is stored at one fixed width, 1, 2 or 4 bytes, set by its widest character, so indexing is O(1) but one emoji widens the whole string. Build text with "".join, not += in a loop.

Q · Mechanism — Explain PEP 393: how CPython picks a representation, and what it means for memory. At creation CPython scans for the highest code point and stores every character at the narrowest width that holds it: 1 byte for ASCII/Latin-1, 2 for the Basic Multilingual Plane, 4 beyond, including emoji. The width never changes because the string never changes, which keeps s[i] and len O(1). The cost: the widest character prices the whole string, 1,041 bytes vs 4,064 on 3.12 for a thousand ASCII characters plus one emoji. And len counts code points, not bytes or visible characters.

Q · Failure — A log job builds output with result += line and runs for hours on big files, though a quick test was fast. Why? Each += copies everything so far, ~n²/2 characters total. The test was fast because the result's only reference was a local, so CPython resized in place. In the real job another reference existed (stored on an object, appended to a list, passed to a logger) or it ran on PyPy, so every append copied; one alias turned 200,000 appends from ~5 ms into ~333 ms (see Break it). Fix: "".join, io.StringIO, or stream lines straight to the output file.

Q · Design — A pipeline handles gigabytes of mostly-ASCII text with occasional emoji and CJK, in front of an LLM. How do string internals shape it? Memory per document is data-dependent, so keep payloads as UTF-8 bytes where a stage only routes or batches, decode only for normalisation, regex or tokenisation, and process per document so one emoji doesn't widen a gigabyte. Each str transform copies, so use single passes: one regex, str.translate, or a Rust tokenizer over bytes. Normalise keys once, then hash to a short digest. Enforce limits in bytes or tokens, never len(str). Watch per-worker memory against the non-ASCII share of traffic.

⚖️ Compare

str bytes bytearray list + join / StringIO
Holds code points octets octets pieces of text
Mutable no no yes yes (the buffer)
Per char 1/2/4 B by widest 1 B 1 B + headroom pieces + list
Hashable yes, cached yes no no
Build n pieces O(n²) with += O(n²) with += amortised O(n) O(n)

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "String concatenation in a loop is fine now"
    ✅ Only while nothing else references the string.
    ↳ Why: CPython's in-place += needs a sole reference; an alias, an attribute target or PyPy makes it O(n²) (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: "".join(parts).
  • 🪞 "A string costs one byte per character"
    ✅ The widest character sets the width for all of them.
    ↳ Symptom: one emoji makes a 1,000-character string ~4× bigger (1,041 → 4,064 bytes on 3.12).
  • ❌ "Equal-looking strings are equal"
    ✅ "é" and "é" render the same but compare unequal.
    ↳ Fix: unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s) before keying, deduplicating or comparing.
  • 🔀 Not the same: str and bytes
    ↳ Difference: str is code points with no encoding; bytes is octets.
    ↳ So: len("😀") is 1 but its UTF-8 is 4 bytes; convert only at I/O edges.
  • ⚠️ Don't rely on interning for correctness.
    ↳ Why: runtime-built strings aren't interned, so is gives random answers.
    ↳ Instead: ==; use sys.intern only to save memory on many repeated keys.
  • ⚠️ Don't enforce byte or token limits with len(str).
    ↳ Why: len counts code points; encoded size and token count can be several times larger.
    ↳ Instead: measure the encoded bytes or the tokenizer's count.
  • 🔖 Version: PEP 393 since 3.3; the empty-string size dropped from 49 to 41 bytes in 3.12 (PEP 623).
    ↳ Note: sizes and timings here are CPython 3.12.13 on arm64; the in-place += trick is CPython-only.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: pyobject-refcounts-object-header — the header and refcount the += shortcut reads · is-vs-equals-identity-interning — interning and identity ⬇️ Next: dict-internals — cached string hashes make cheap keys · text-processing-unicode — normalisation and encodings in practice

notes.title: Attribute Lookup & the MRO
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Data model: customizing attribute access · 📘 Descriptor HowTo: invocation from an instance · 📘 The Python 2.3 MRO (C3) · 📘 super · 🔬 Ten Thousand Meters: how attributes work · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Method resolution order

⚡ TL;DR

Lookup order: data descriptor on the class → instance __dict__ → non-data descriptor or class attribute → __getattr__. The class is searched along the MRO, and super() means "next in the MRO", not "my parent".

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Full lookup order for obj.x? Data descriptor → instance __dict__ → non-data/class attr → __getattr__.
Why does a property beat the instance dict? It's a data descriptor (defines __set__), checked first.
__getattribute__ vs __getattr__? Every access vs only after normal lookup fails.
What does C3 guarantee? Children before parents; each class statement's base order kept.
What does super() find? The next class after the current one in type(self).__mro__.
Does obj.x = v change a class attribute? No: data descriptor __set__, else write to obj.__dict__.

💡 The idea

"The instance dict wins, then the class" is the rule most people carry. Push on it:

class Account:
    kind = "standard"                  # plain class attribute
    @property
    def balance(self): return 100      # data descriptor
    def close(self): return "closed"   # non-data descriptor (a function)

a = Account()
a.__dict__.update(kind="gold", balance=-1, close="not a method")
a.kind, a.balance, a.close             # → ('gold', 100, 'not a method')

The instance won for kind and close but lost for balance. The difference is what the class holds: a data descriptor (defines __set__ or __delete__, like property) outranks the instance; a non-data descriptor (only __get__, like a function) or a plain value comes after it (#25). That's also how a method gets accidentally shadowed by an attribute of the same name.

The trade: a class can take control of an attribute for every instance (properties, slots, ORM fields), at the cost of a lookup order that isn't simply "instance, then class".

⚙️ How it works

obj.x calls type(obj).__getattribute__(obj, "x"), which for ordinary classes is object.__getattribute__:

The class is searched first. Python must know whether the class has a data descriptor for the name before it may trust the instance dict, so every read starts with an MRO walk. In CPython a versioned per-type attribute cache makes that walk usually one hit, and since 3.11 specialised bytecodes (LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE and friends) skip most of the generic path.

__getattribute__ vs __getattr__. __getattribute__ runs on every access and implements the whole flow; overriding it is rare and slow. __getattr__ runs only after normal lookup raises AttributeError, so it's the safe hook for proxies, fallbacks and lazy attributes.

C3 fixes the MRO once per class. For the diamond class D(B, C) with B and C both inheriting A, C3 gives D → B → C → A → object: every class before its bases, each statement's base order kept, A once. If no order satisfies both rules, the class statement fails with Cannot create a consistent method resolution order.

super() is "next in the MRO"; setting is simpler. In a method of B on a D instance, super() continues after B, reaching C, a class B never inherited from. That's cooperative multiple inheritance. obj.x = v only checks for a data descriptor's __set__, otherwise writes obj.__dict__; it never changes a class attribute.

💻 Code

A delegating proxy and a cooperative super() chain:

class MeteredClient:
    """Wrap any SDK client; count calls without re-declaring its API."""
    def __init__(self, inner):
        self._inner, self.calls = inner, 0       # found normally: never reaches __getattr__
    def __getattr__(self, name):                 # ONLY for names we don't define
        if name.startswith("_"):                 # copy/pickle probe before __init__: avoid recursion
            raise AttributeError(name)
        attr = getattr(self._inner, name)
        if not callable(attr):
            return attr
        def counted(*a, **kw):
            self.calls += 1
            return attr(*a, **kw)
        return counted

class Base:
    def setup(self): return ["Base"]
class Cache(Base):
    def setup(self): return ["Cache"] + super().setup()      # next in the MRO, not Base
class Metrics(Base):
    def setup(self): return ["Metrics"] + super().setup()
class Service(Cache, Metrics):
    def setup(self): return ["Service"] + super().setup()

print([c.__name__ for c in Service.__mro__])   # → ['Service', 'Cache', 'Metrics', 'Base', 'object']
print(Service().setup())                       # → ['Service', 'Cache', 'Metrics', 'Base']

Without the underscore guard, copy.copy(client) builds an instance without running __init__, reaches self._inner inside __getattr__, and recurses into RecursionError.

⚠️ Break it: one class in the chain calls its parent directly.

class A:
    def hi(self): return ["A"]
class B(A):
    def hi(self): return ["B"] + A.hi(self)          # ❌ hard-coded parent
class C(A):
    def hi(self): return ["C"] + super().hi()
class D(B, C):
    def hi(self): return ["D"] + super().hi()
print(D().hi())
# look for: C missing from the result
# naive model predicts: ['D', 'B', 'C', 'A'], because C is in D's MRO

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints ['D', 'B', 'A']. B skipped "next in the MRO" (C) by naming A, so every class after B in the chain was silently skipped.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: obj.x searches the class's MRO first, because a data descriptor there, like a property or a slot, takes priority over the instance. If there isn't one, the instance dict wins, then non-data descriptors such as methods or plain class attributes, then __getattr__ as a last resort. The MRO comes from C3 linearisation, and super() means "next class in that order", which is what makes cooperative multiple inheritance work.

Q · Mechanism — Explain C3 and what super() does in a diamond. C3 builds a list for each class that keeps every class before its bases and preserves the base order written in each class statement, merging the parents' lists. For D(B, C) over A that's D, B, C, A, object. super() in B.method, called on a D, finds B in type(self).__mro__ and continues from the next class, C, not A. If every class calls super() once, each method runs exactly once; if C3 can't satisfy both rules, class creation fails.

Q · Failure — After adding a mixin, some initialisation code stopped running in one subclass, with no error. Diagnose. A class in the hierarchy calls its parent explicitly (Base.__init__(self)) instead of super().__init__(). Adding the mixin changed the MRO so that the mixin now sits after that class, and the hard-coded call jumps straight to Base, skipping it (see Break it). Tests on the old hierarchy passed. Fix: super() everywhere in the chain, **kwargs passed through so each class takes its own arguments, and a test asserting every setup ran once.

Q · Design — A plugin framework lets teams combine behaviour classes (auth, caching, metrics) through multiple inheritance. Where does it break, and what would you do? The MRO is the binding constraint: behaviour order is decided by base order in every subclass, so two teams' combinations can order the same mixins differently, and one direct parent call breaks the chain. It breaks on incompatible orders (a TypeError at import) and on mixins with clashing attribute names. I'd cap mixins at small, single-purpose, super()-cooperative classes, prefer composition for anything stateful, and add a test that prints each plugin's MRO. Watch for silently skipped setup calls first.

⚖️ Compare

__getattribute__ __getattr__ data descriptor non-data descriptor
When it runs every access after lookup fails before instance dict after instance dict
Typical use rare: full control proxies, fallbacks property, slots, ORM fields methods, classmethod
Defines the method the method __get__ + __set__/__delete__ __get__ only
Risk slow, recursion recursion before __init__ — shadowed by instance attrs

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "The instance dict always wins"
    ✅ A data descriptor on the class wins first.
    ↳ Why: property, slots and ORM fields define __set__, so they're checked before the instance dict.
    ↳ Proof: a.balance returns 100 despite balance=-1 in a.__dict__.
  • 🪞 "super() calls my parent class"
    ✅ It calls the next class in type(self).__mro__.
    ↳ Why it matters: in a diamond that's a sibling, which is how cooperative multiple inheritance visits every class once.
  • ❌ "obj.x = v updates the class attribute x"
    ✅ It writes the instance dict, unless a data descriptor's __set__ intercepts.
    ↳ Symptom: the class value is shadowed for that instance only, silently.
  • 🔀 Not the same: __getattribute__ and __getattr__
    ↳ Difference: __getattribute__ runs on every access; __getattr__ only after lookup fails.
    ↳ So: override __getattr__ for proxies; overriding __getattribute__ slows every attribute read.
  • ⚠️ Don't call a parent method by class name in a cooperative hierarchy.
    ↳ Why: it skips every class between you and that parent in the MRO (see Break it).
    ↳ Instead: super() in every class, passing **kwargs through.
  • ⚠️ Don't touch self.<attr> inside __getattr__ without a guard.
    ↳ Why: copy and pickle create instances without __init__, so the attribute is missing and __getattr__ recurses.
    ↳ Instead: reject underscore names, or read via self.__dict__.
  • 🔖 Version: C3 has been the MRO since 2.3; specialised LOAD_ATTR_* bytecodes since 3.11.
    ↳ Also: the behaviour is language-level; the attribute cache and specialisation are CPython speedups.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: dict-internals — instance and class __dict__s are what lookup searches · data-model-dunder-protocols — special methods are looked up on the type ⬇️ Next: descriptors — the data / non-data rule in depth · metaclasses-class-creation — where the MRO is computed

notes.title: Descriptors
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Descriptor HowTo Guide · 📘 Data model: implementing descriptors · 📘 __set_name__ · 📘 property · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Descriptor in Python

⚡ TL;DR

A descriptor is an object on a class whose __get__ / __set__ run when you touch that name on an instance. Data descriptors (__set__) beat the instance dict; non-data ones (__get__ only, like functions) lose to it.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What makes an object a descriptor? Its type defines __get__, __set__ or __delete__, and it sits on a class.
Data vs non-data? Has __set__/__delete__ → beats instance dict; __get__ only → loses.
How do methods bind self? Functions are non-data descriptors; __get__ returns a bound method.
What does __set_name__ give you? The attribute name the descriptor was assigned to, at class creation.
Where must per-instance state live? On the instance (obj.__dict__), never on the shared descriptor.
Why does cached_property work? Non-data: first read stores in the instance dict, which then wins.

💡 The idea

A plain attribute runs no code on assignment, so o.qty = -1 slips straight in. Put the rule in an object on the class instead:

class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name): self.private = "_" + name   # learns its own name
    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        return self if obj is None else getattr(obj, self.private)
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value <= 0: raise ValueError(f"{self.private[1:]} must be > 0, got {value}")
        setattr(obj, self.private, value)

class Order:
    qty = Positive()                     # a descriptor on the CLASS
    def __init__(self, qty): self.qty = qty

o = Order(3)
o.qty = -1                               # → ValueError: qty must be > 0, got -1
vars(o)                                  # → {'_qty': 3}

Assigning o.qty called Positive.__set__, which validated and stored under _qty; the instance dict doesn't even contain qty.

The trade: an attribute's behaviour is written once on the class and reused everywhere, and every access becomes a method call you have to reason about.

⚙️ How it works

The attribute lookup (#24) is what calls the descriptor's methods:

One descriptor per class attribute, shared by every instance. __get__(self, obj, objtype) gets the instance as obj (None when read on the class, where convention returns the descriptor itself). __set__(self, obj, value) and __delete__(self, obj) handle writes and deletes. Since self is shared, per-instance data must live on obj.

Data vs non-data decides precedence. __set__ or __delete__ makes a data descriptor that outranks the instance dict. __get__ alone makes a non-data descriptor that the instance dict overrides. __set_name__ (3.6+) is called at class creation with the assigned name, so qty = Positive("qty") is no longer needed.

Functions are non-data descriptors: that's how methods work. A function in a class body is stored as a plain function; function.__get__(obj, type) returns a bound method packaging it with obj. That's why obj.method and Cls.method differ, and why an instance attribute can shadow a method.

The built-ins are descriptors. property is a C data descriptor whose __set__ raises if you gave no setter. classmethod binds to the class, staticmethod returns the plain function, __slots__ creates a member_descriptor per slot (#5), and functools.cached_property is deliberately non-data so its cached value in the instance dict wins after the first read.

💻 Code

A reusable typed field, the shape ORMs and settings libraries use:

class Field:
    """Data descriptor: coerce + validate on every assignment, stored per instance."""
    def __init__(self, kind, *, min_value=None):
        self.kind, self.min_value = kind, min_value
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):              # once, at class creation
        self.name, self.storage = name, "_" + name
    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self                               # Model.port → the Field, for introspection
        return obj.__dict__[self.storage]             # per-INSTANCE storage
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        value = self.kind(value)                      # coerce: "8080" → 8080
        if self.min_value is not None and value < self.min_value:
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name}={value} below {self.min_value}")
        obj.__dict__[self.storage] = value

class ServerConfig:
    port, workers = Field(int, min_value=1), Field(int, min_value=1)
    def __init__(self, port, workers):
        self.port, self.workers = port, workers       # both go through Field.__set__

cfg = ServerConfig("8080", 4)
print(cfg.port, type(cfg.port).__name__)              # → 8080 int
print([n for n, v in vars(ServerConfig).items() if isinstance(v, Field)])   # → ['port', 'workers']

Returning self for obj is None is what lets the last line find all fields, which is how ORMs build a schema from class attributes.

⚠️ Break it: store the value on the descriptor.

class Balance:
    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None): return self.value    # ❌ state on the descriptor
    def __set__(self, obj, value): self.value = value          # ❌ shared by ALL instances
class Account:
    balance = Balance()
a, b = Account(), Account()
a.balance = 100
b.balance = 5
print(a.balance)
# look for: 5, because b's write overwrote a's value
# naive model predicts: 100, since a and b are separate objects

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints 5. There's one descriptor per class attribute; self is that shared object, and per-instance data belongs on obj.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A descriptor is an object stored on a class whose type defines __get__, __set__ or __delete__; attribute lookup calls those methods when you read or write that name on an instance. Data descriptors, with __set__, take priority over the instance dict; non-data ones, with only __get__, don't. Methods, property, classmethod, staticmethod and __slots__ are all descriptors, which is how functions become bound methods.

Q · Mechanism — How does obj.method become a bound method, and why can an instance attribute shadow it? The function is stored on the class. Lookup finds it on the MRO; it isn't a data descriptor, so the instance dict is checked first. If the name isn't there, CPython calls function.__get__(obj, type(obj)), which returns a bound method holding the function and obj, so calling it passes obj as self. Because functions are non-data, assigning obj.method = 1 puts a value in the instance dict that wins from then on. A property can't be shadowed that way: it defines __set__.

Q · Failure — A custom validator descriptor works in tests but in production values leak between objects. Diagnose. The descriptor stores state on self (see Break it). Tests created one instance, so they passed; in production every instance shares one descriptor, so the last write wins for everyone, a cross-request data leak. Fix: store per instance in obj.__dict__ under a private name learned from __set_name__, or a WeakKeyDictionary keyed by obj for objects without __dict__. Add a test with two instances asserting independence.

Q · Design — You're designing a settings or ORM layer where fields declare type, default and validation. Descriptors, __init_subclass__, or a metaclass? Per-attribute behaviour is the binding constraint, so fields are data descriptors: coercion and validation on __set__, names from __set_name__, storage in the instance. Class-level registration (collecting fields into a schema) is __init_subclass__ or a scan of vars(cls), not a metaclass, which conflicts with other metaclasses. For new code I'd also ask whether pydantic or dataclasses already give this. Watch per-attribute access cost in hot paths first: every read is a Python call.

⚖️ Compare

property custom data descriptor cached_property __slots__ member
Kind data data non-data data
Reuse across attributes no, one per attribute yes, one class many fields per attribute automatic
Stores value wherever the getter reads where you put it (instance) instance __dict__ fixed offset in object
Typical use computed or guarded attribute validated fields, ORM columns expensive lazy value memory layout

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A descriptor is a property"
    ✅ property is one descriptor; any object with __get__/__set__/__delete__ on a class is one.
    ↳ Why it matters: functions, classmethod, staticmethod and slots all use the same protocol.
  • 🪞 "I can keep the value on self inside the descriptor"
    ✅ self is shared by every instance.
    ↳ Symptom: one object's write overwrites everyone's (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: store in obj.__dict__ under a private name.
  • ❌ "A descriptor works as an instance attribute too"
    ✅ Only when found on the class.
    ↳ Why: lookup calls __get__ only for class-level objects; on an instance it's just a value.
  • 🔀 Not the same: data and non-data descriptors
    ↳ Difference: __set__/__delete__ → beats the instance dict; __get__ only → instance dict wins.
    ↳ Example: that's why cached_property can cache in the instance and property can't be shadowed.
  • ⚠️ Don't forget obj is None in __get__.
    ↳ Why: reading the attribute on the class passes None, and code that dereferences it crashes introspection, docs tools and ORMs.
    ↳ Fix: if obj is None: return self.
  • ⚠️ Don't reach for a descriptor when property or a dataclass field will do.
    ↳ Why: every access becomes a Python-level call, and readers must know the protocol.
    ↳ Instead: descriptors for behaviour reused across many attributes or classes.
  • 🔖 Version: __set_name__ is 3.6+; cached_property 3.8+ and lock-free since 3.12.
    ↳ Before 3.6: the descriptor had to be told its name or use a metaclass.

notes.title: Metaclasses & Class Creation
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Data model: customizing class creation · 📜 PEP 487: Simpler class-creation customisation · 📘 type · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Metaclasses

⚡ TL;DR

A class statement runs its body into a namespace, then calls type(name, bases, ns); a metaclass replaces type. Since 3.6, __init_subclass__ and __set_name__ cover most of what metaclasses were used for, and they compose.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a class statement actually do? Runs the body into a namespace, then calls metaclass(name, bases, ns).
What replaced most metaclass uses in 3.6? __init_subclass__ and __set_name__ (PEP 487).
What can only a metaclass do? __prepare__ (custom namespace), class-object behaviour (__call__, operators).

💡 The idea

A class feels like a declaration, but it's an object built by running code, and you can build one without a class statement:

class Plugin:
    name = "base"
type(Plugin)                                                     # → <class 'type'>
Dyn = type("Dyn", (object,), {"name": "dyn", "run": lambda self: self.name})
Dyn().run()                                                      # → 'dyn'

A metaclass swaps type for your subclass of type, so code runs whenever a class using it is created. The common reason, registering subclasses, now has a lighter hook that runs at the same moment:

class Plugin:
    plugins = {}
    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, name=None, **kw):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kw)
        Plugin.plugins[name or cls.__name__] = cls
class CsvPlugin(Plugin, name="csv"): ...
Plugin.plugins                                                   # → {'csv': <class '__main__.CsvPlugin'>}

The trade: a metaclass gives full control over class creation, at the cost of being contagious to every subclass and conflicting with other metaclasses, while __init_subclass__ covers most uses and composes.

⚙️ How it works

The creation sequence. Python picks the metaclass (explicit, else the most derived of the bases' metaclasses), calls M.__prepare__ for the namespace (usually a dict), executes the body into it, then calls M.__new__(M, name, bases, ns, **kw). Inside type.__new__, __set_name__ runs on each attribute that defines it, then the parent's __init_subclass__. Then M.__init__, then class decorators, then the name is bound.

Why the light hooks need no metaclass. __set_name__ and __init_subclass__ run inside type.__new__, so every class built by type gets them. Measured on CPython 3.12 with a custom metaclass, a descriptor and a parent hook, the order is: Meta.__new__ starts → __set_name__ → __init_subclass__ → back in Meta.__new__.

Class keywords flow through. class C(Base, key="x") passes key to the metaclass's __new__ and on to __init_subclass__, so a metaclass that doesn't accept and forward **kw breaks every class using it.

__prepare__ is metaclass-only. It chooses the namespace object the body runs in, which is how enum detects duplicate member names.

💻 Code

A plugin registry validated at import time, with no metaclass:

class Exporter:
    registry: dict[str, type["Exporter"]] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, fmt: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)            # cooperative with other bases
        if not callable(getattr(cls, "export", None)):
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__} must define export()")   # fails at import, in CI
        if fmt in Exporter.registry:
            raise TypeError(f"duplicate exporter for {fmt!r}")
        Exporter.registry[fmt] = cls

    def export(self, rows): raise NotImplementedError

class CsvExporter(Exporter, fmt="csv"):
    def export(self, rows): return "\n".join(",".join(map(str, r)) for r in rows)

print(Exporter.registry["csv"]().export([(1, 2), (3, 4)]))   # → 1,2 (newline) 3,4

The value is when it runs: a missing method or duplicate format fails when the module is imported, not on the first request that needs it.

⚠️ Break it: mix two metaclasses.

class MetaA(type): pass
class MetaB(type): pass
class A(metaclass=MetaA): pass
class B(metaclass=MetaB): pass
class C(A, B): pass
# look for: TypeError at the class statement
# naive model predicts: C builds fine, like any multiple inheritance

On CPython 3.12.13 it raises TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases. Neither metaclass is a subclass of the other, so Python can't pick one; that's why metaclasses are contagious and libraries avoid them.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A metaclass is the type of a class: whatever builds the class object, type by default. A class statement runs its body into a namespace and calls the metaclass with the name, bases and namespace, so a custom metaclass runs code at class creation. I'd use one rarely: registration, subclass validation and attribute naming are covered by __init_subclass__, __set_name__ and class decorators, which compose where metaclasses conflict.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through what happens when Python executes class C(Base, key="x"):. It determines the metaclass, explicit or the most derived among the bases', and calls __prepare__ for a namespace. It executes the body into that namespace, then calls M.__new__(M, "C", (Base,), ns, key="x"). Inside type.__new__, attributes defining __set_name__ learn their names, then Base.__init_subclass__(key="x") runs. Then M.__init__, class decorators, and finally the name C is bound. A metaclass that doesn't forward **kw breaks the key argument.

⚖️ Compare

Metaclass __init_subclass__ Class decorator __set_name__
Runs at class creation at subclass creation after the class exists at class creation, per attribute
Affects every class using it, inherited subclasses of the base the one decorated class one descriptor
Composes conflicts with other metaclasses yes, via super() yes, stackable yes
Use for __prepare__, class-object behaviour registries, validation one-off transforms descriptor naming

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Metaclasses are how you register or validate subclasses"
    ✅ __init_subclass__ does that, with no metaclass.
    ↳ Why: it runs inside type.__new__ at the same moment, and composes with other bases.
  • 🔀 Not the same: __new__ on a class and on a metaclass
    ↳ Difference: a class's __new__ builds instances; a metaclass's __new__ builds classes.
    ↳ Tell: the metaclass __new__ receives (name, bases, namespace).
  • ⚠️ Don't add a metaclass to a library's public base class.
    ↳ Why: every user subclass inherits it, and combining with another library's metaclass raises a conflict (see Break it).
    ↳ Instead: __init_subclass__, __set_name__ or a decorator.
  • ⚠️ Don't write a metaclass __new__ without **kwargs.
    ↳ Symptom: any class keyword (class C(Base, fmt="csv")) raises unexpected keyword argument.
    ↳ Fix: accept and forward **kw to super().__new__.
  • ⚠️ Don't do heavy work at class creation.
    ↳ Why: it runs at import, slowing startup and every test run, and failures look like import errors.
    ↳ Instead: validate cheaply at creation, defer expensive setup to first use.
  • 🔖 Version: __init_subclass__ and __set_name__ are 3.6+ (PEP 487).
    ↳ So: older code that uses metaclasses only for registration can usually be simplified.

🔗 Links

notes.title: Bytecode & the Evaluation Loop
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 dis: disassembler for Python bytecode · 📘 Data model: code objects · 📜 PEP 659: Specializing adaptive interpreter · 📖 Ten Thousand Meters: how bytecode is executed

⚡ TL;DR

CPython compiles source to bytecode once, then a stack-machine loop runs it one instruction at a time. Since 3.11, hot instructions that keep seeing the same types are rewritten in place to faster, typed forms.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Source to execution? Source → tokens → AST → bytecode in a code object (cached as .pyc) → eval loop.
What is the eval loop? A stack machine: fetch an instruction, run it on the frame's value stack, repeat.
What did PEP 659 (3.11) change? Hot, type-stable instructions are specialised in place, with de-optimisation on type change.

💡 The idea

"Python runs the source" can't explain why locals are faster than globals or where the GIL switches threads. Ask what it actually runs (CPython 3.12):

import dis
def add(a, b): return a + b
dis.dis(add)                      # → LOAD_FAST a · LOAD_FAST b · BINARY_OP (+) · RETURN_VALUE
add(1, 2); add(1, 2)
dis.dis(add, adaptive=True)       # → LOAD_FAST__LOAD_FAST · LOAD_FAST · BINARY_OP_ADD_INT · RETURN_VALUE

def compiled the body to bytecode on a code object (add.__code__); the source isn't consulted at run time. After two calls the generic BINARY_OP was rewritten to BINARY_OP_ADD_INT, which assumes ints and skips the general dispatch. Called with strings, it re-specialised to BINARY_OP_ADD_UNICODE after 53 calls on 3.12.

The trade: a compact, generic instruction set keeps CPython simple and portable, and the adaptive specialiser buys speed back by rewriting hot instructions for the types it actually sees.

⚙️ How it works

Code objects are the unit of compiled code. Every function, class body, module and comprehension has one, holding the bytecode (co_code), constants (co_consts), local names (co_varnames), stack depth and the line table for tracebacks. They're immutable; a function is a code object plus globals, defaults and closure cells.

The eval loop is a stack machine. In CPython, _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault fetches an instruction, jumps to its handler, repeats. Locals are an array, so LOAD_FAST 0 is one read; a global is a dict lookup in LOAD_GLOBAL. That's why locals are faster, and why "cache a global in a local" was a classic trick, much less needed since 3.11.

Specialisation (PEP 659, 3.11+). Instructions carry inline caches and counters. After a short warm-up, one that keeps seeing the same types becomes BINARY_OP_ADD_INT, LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE or FOR_ITER_LIST; each checks its assumption cheaply and de-optimises if it fails, with a back-off before trying again. It's still an interpreter, not a JIT, so type-stable hot code gains most.

The GIL switches between instructions. The loop checks for a pending GIL request after the switch interval (sys.getswitchinterval(), 0.005 s by default), so a thread can lose the GIL between any two instructions (#33). Bytecode is a CPython detail: opcodes change between minor versions, which is why .pyc files carry a version tag.

💻 Code

The everyday use of dis: seeing why += on shared state isn't thread-safe.

import dis, threading

counter = 0
def hit():
    global counter
    counter += 1               # looks like one step

dis.dis(hit)
# → LOAD_GLOBAL counter      1. read
# → LOAD_CONST 1
# → BINARY_OP 13 (+=)        2. compute
# → STORE_GLOBAL counter     3. write back
# the GIL can switch between any two: two threads read 5, both write 6

lock = threading.Lock()
def safe_hit():
    global counter
    with lock:                 # the fix is a lock, not "the GIL protects me"
        counter += 1

It turns "the GIL makes Python thread-safe" into a visible three-instruction race.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: CPython tokenises and parses source into an AST, compiles it to bytecode on a code object, and caches that as a .pyc. The eval loop is a stack machine that runs one instruction at a time against the frame's value stack. Since 3.11 the interpreter is adaptive: hot instructions that keep seeing the same types are rewritten to specialised forms like BINARY_OP_ADD_INT, and fall back if the types change. No JIT is involved.

Q · Mechanism — Explain the stack-based eval loop and what PEP 659 changed. Each instruction manipulates the value stack: LOAD_FAST pushes a local by index, LOAD_GLOBAL looks up the globals and builtins dicts, BINARY_OP pops two operands and pushes the result. Because types are dynamic, a generic BINARY_OP inspects operand types and dispatches through the type's slot every time; that, plus refcounting and boxing, is the interpreter overhead. PEP 659 adds inline caches and rewrites type-stable instructions in place to guarded fast paths that de-optimise on a miss, so monomorphic hot loops speed up and polymorphic ones less.

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Python interprets the source line by line"
    ✅ It compiles the whole module to bytecode first, then runs the bytecode.
    ↳ Proof: a SyntaxError anywhere stops the module before line 1 runs.
  • 🪞 "The GIL makes counter += 1 thread-safe"
    ✅ It's several instructions, and the GIL can switch between them.
    ↳ Symptom: lost updates under threads, rare enough to pass tests.
    ↳ Fix: a threading.Lock, or a thread-safe structure.
  • ❌ "3.11+ has a JIT"
    ✅ 3.11's speedup is specialisation inside the interpreter.
    ↳ Note: an experimental copy-and-patch JIT arrived as a build option in 3.13; it isn't what PEP 659 is.
  • 🔀 Not the same: code object and function
    ↳ Difference: a code object is immutable compiled code; a function wraps it with globals, defaults and closure cells.
    ↳ Example: two closures from one def share one code object but have different cells.
  • ⚠️ Don't depend on specific opcodes or .pyc files across versions.
    ↳ Why: opcodes are added, renamed and removed between minor releases, and .pyc is version-tagged.
    ↳ Instead: treat dis output as a diagnostic for your interpreter only.
  • 🔖 Version: specialisation since 3.11; on 3.12, add(1, 2) specialised after 2 calls and re-specialised to strings after 53.
    ↳ So: warm-up counts and opcode names are 3.12 details; re-check on your version.
